articles.title: Why the programme is built to be handed over
articles.blurb: The aim is a patient who no longer needs the appointments, not one who keeps them.
articles.desc: Why Rayhab builds scoliosis programmes designed to be run independently, with periodic review, rather than open-ended clinic attendance.
articles.stand: Scoliosis is managed over years. Any plan that depends on you being in a clinic twice a week for those years is not a plan.
key: The programme is designed from the first session to be run by you at home.
Clinic sessions teach, correct and progress. They are not where the volume happens.
Independence is treated as an outcome and reviewed like any other.
Periodic review replaces indefinite attendance.

blocks.t: Start from the timescale

A curve found at thirteen is managed through a growth spurt, into skeletal maturity, and then for the rest of adult life. That is a horizon measured in years and decades, not in a block of six sessions.

Once you accept that timescale, a lot follows. Whatever is prescribed has to be sustainable without supervision, affordable in time, and robust enough to survive exams, holidays, injuries and periods of low motivation.
What clinic time is actually for

items: **Teaching** the correction, which needs hands and feedback and cannot be learned from a sheet.
**Correcting drift**, because every home programme decays in predictable ways.
**Progressing**, adding difficulty, load or duration once something is reliable.
**Re-measuring**, so changes are recorded rather than remembered.

blocks.t: None of those require weekly attendance indefinitely. They require attendance at the right moments.
Designing for handover

A programme built to be handed over looks different from one built to be supervised. It is shorter. It uses equipment you actually have. It has a clearly marked minimum version for bad weeks. And it is written down in a form you can follow when you have forgotten what the cue meant.
A programme that takes forty minutes and needs a studio will be abandoned, and an abandoned programme has no effect at all. A shorter programme that is actually done beats a better one that is not.
Independence as an outcome

At review the questions are not only about the curve. Can you produce the correction without cueing? Can you tell when you have lost it? Do you know which part of the programme to drop first when the week collapses, and which part never to drop?
If the answer to those is yes, the programme has been handed over successfully, whatever the angle is doing.

articles.title: Getting a teenager to actually do their exercises
articles.blurb: The most common reason a good programme fails has nothing to do with the programme.
articles.desc: Practical approaches for adherence to a scoliosis home programme in adolescents, and why nagging tends to make things worse.
articles.stand: Written for parents, with the awkward part said first: the more this becomes your project, the less likely it is to work.
key: Adherence, not programme design, is usually what decides the outcome.
Ownership has to transfer to the teenager, which means tolerating an imperfect version done independently.
Short and daily beats long and occasional.
Attach it to something that already happens rather than finding new time.

blocks.t: The actual problem
Most home programmes are not abandoned because they were wrong. They are abandoned because they were long, boring, easy to forget, and belonged to a parent rather than to the person doing them.
A teenager who is managing their own condition imperfectly is in a better position than one whose parent is managing it perfectly, because only one of those situations survives them leaving home.
Make it small enough to survive a bad week

Ask for a version that takes ten to fifteen minutes and can be done in a bedroom. Ask explicitly which parts are the minimum on a bad day. Having a sanctioned reduced version prevents the common pattern where one missed session becomes a missed month.
Attach it to an existing habit
New habits attach far better to existing ones than to a time of day. Before a shower. After brushing teeth. While a series is loading. The cue does the remembering so nobody has to.
What actually helps from a parent

items: Ask **whether it happened**, not whether it was done properly. Quality is the clinician's job.
Keep the equipment permanently set up. Friction is the enemy.
Let them own the review. Have them describe their own programme at the appointment.
Notice things other than the curve: standing taller, carrying a bag better, less fatigue by evening.

blocks.t: What tends to backfire

items: Daily reminders that turn into an argument. The programme becomes the argument.
Framing it around appearance. It is reliably the fastest way to make a teenager disengage.
Threats about surgery. Frightening someone is not motivation, and it damages trust.
Correcting their posture in public.

blocks.t: The honest framing

Adolescents respond better to being treated as the person responsible than as the object of a project. Telling them plainly what the programme is for, what it can and cannot do, and that the decision to do it is genuinely theirs tends to work better than any reminder system.
It also happens to be true, which helps.

articles.title: Can you lift weights with scoliosis?
articles.blurb: Usually yes, and avoiding load entirely tends to cost more than it saves.
articles.desc: Whether resistance training is safe with scoliosis, what to adjust, and why building strength supports rather than threatens a curved spine.
articles.stand: Short answer: for most people with a curve, yes. The longer answer is about how, not whether.
key: There is no good evidence that resistance training worsens an idiopathic curve.
Strength is what lets a correction hold up under real-world load.
Asymmetry needs attention: unilateral work is useful, and load tolerance may differ side to side.
Coaching quality matters more than exercise selection.

blocks.t: Where the worry comes from

The reasoning sounds sensible: a curve is a structural weakness, load makes structural things worse, so avoid load. The reasoning does not hold up. Bone and soft tissue adapt to load, and avoiding it produces a spine with less capacity, not a safer one.
There is no good evidence that appropriately coached resistance training causes idiopathic curves to progress.
Why it actively helps
A correction you can hold for thirty seconds lying down and lose the moment you pick up a bag is not much use. Strength through the trunk, hips and shoulders is what carries a correction into a day.
For adults especially, capacity is usually the limiting factor in what someone can tolerate, and building it is one of the more reliable things rehabilitation can offer.
What actually gets adjusted

items: **Unilateral work.** Single-arm and single-leg variations expose and address side-to-side differences that a barbell hides.
**Position first, load second.** Establish the corrected position, then add weight to it.
**Breathing.** Holding the corrective breathing pattern under load is a skill, and heavy bracing changes it. Both are taught.
**Load tolerance may differ by side**, and that is worth tracking rather than ignoring.

blocks.t: The lifts people ask about

Heavy overhead pressing, deadlifts and squats are not banned by default. They are loaded spinal tasks that need competent positioning, sensible progression and attention to how you tolerate them. Plenty of people with curves perform all three.
What warrants more caution is maximal loading under fatigue with poor positioning, which is a reasonable caution for anyone.
When to get it looked at
New or escalating pain with a specific lift, symptoms travelling into an arm or leg, or a sense that one side is losing capacity are all reasons to have it assessed rather than trained through.

Whether particular sports or loading patterns influence curve progression is not well established. Associations have been reported in some activities, but the evidence does not support telling people to stop training.

articles.title: Working alongside a brace
articles.blurb: Bracing and exercise are not alternatives, and treating them as rivals helps nobody.
articles.desc: How scoliosis-specific exercise works alongside brace treatment, what the evidence for bracing shows, and how the two are coordinated.
articles.stand: Families are often presented with bracing and exercise as a choice. In current practice they are usually combined.
key: Bracing has the strongest evidence of any non-surgical treatment for reducing progression to surgical thresholds.
Wear time is the main determinant of whether a brace works.
Exercise alongside bracing helps maintain strength and mobility and supports the correction out of the brace.
The two are coordinated, not opposed.

blocks.t: What bracing is for

A brace does not straighten a spine permanently. Its purpose is to reduce the chance that a growing curve progresses to the point where surgery is considered. It is a growth-window intervention, which is why it is prescribed for skeletally immature patients.

The evidence here is stronger than for most things in scoliosis care. A landmark randomised trial found bracing significantly reduced progression to the surgical threshold compared with observation, and found a clear relationship between hours worn and success.
Wear time is the variable that matters

That same relationship is the most useful thing a family can know. More hours produced better outcomes, with substantial benefit at high daily wear. Prescriptions in the range of 18 to 23 hours a day are common, and results fall away as wear falls.
This makes adherence, not brace design, the usual difference between a brace that works and one that does not.
Where exercise fits

items: **Maintaining strength and mobility** in a trunk that spends most of the day supported.
**Practising the correction out of the brace**, so the shape is actively held rather than only externally imposed.
**Breathing work**, since a brace restricts the ribcage and chest mobility deserves attention.
**Keeping the person moving**, which matters for morale as much as for the spine.

blocks.t: International guidance supports combining scoliosis-specific exercise with bracing rather than choosing between them.
The practical side
Corrective exercises are usually performed out of the brace, during the daily time it is off. That time is limited, which is another argument for a short, well-prioritised programme.

Skin irritation, sleep disruption and the social weight of wearing a brace at school are all real and worth raising with the prescribing team. They are common reasons wear time quietly drops, and they are often fixable.
Whether adding scoliosis-specific exercise to bracing improves the final curve outcome, as opposed to improving strength, mobility and how people cope, has not been definitively established.

articles.title: Returning to sport with a known curve
articles.blurb: The question is rarely whether. It is on what terms, and against which criteria.
articles.desc: How return to sport is managed with scoliosis, why criteria beat calendars, and what to adjust in asymmetric and high-load sports.
articles.stand: Most people with scoliosis can play most sports. Where it goes wrong is stopping entirely, or returning without a plan.
key: Sport is generally encouraged. Withdrawal from activity carries its own cost.
Return is decided by **criteria**, not by a number of weeks.
Asymmetric sports are not banned. They are balanced with deliberate work on the other side.
The corrective programme continues through the season, usually in a reduced form.

blocks.t: The default is to keep playing

There is no good evidence that a curve makes ordinary sport unsafe, and the costs of stopping are real: lost fitness, lost strength, lost social contact, and a teenager who now thinks of themselves as fragile.
That last one is the most expensive and the least discussed.
Criteria rather than a calendar
If sport has been paused, for pain, a flare, or a period of intensive treatment, return should be decided by what someone can demonstrate, not by how many weeks have passed.

items: Can the corrective position be held under the loads the sport demands?
Is side-to-side capacity reasonably matched in the tests that matter for that sport?
Does the trunk hold up when fatigued, not just when fresh?
Do symptoms settle within a day after a hard session, rather than accumulating?

blocks.t: Asymmetric sports
Tennis, swimming with a dominant breathing side, throwing sports, fencing, golf and rowing all load one side differently. Families sometimes ask whether these should be stopped.

Usually not. The evidence that asymmetric sport drives curve progression is weak. The practical answer is to keep the sport and deliberately train the other side, so the total loading across the week is less lopsided than the sport alone.
Through a season

The corrective programme does not stop for the season; it shrinks. A reduced daily version that survives training and travel is far more valuable than a full programme suspended for four months and restarted badly.
Plan the in-season version before the season starts, while there is still attention available to plan it.

articles.title: Your child was just diagnosed. What now?
articles.blurb: The first week is mostly about not making decisions under pressure.
articles.desc: What to do in the days after an adolescent scoliosis diagnosis: what to ask, what to gather, what can wait, and what genuinely cannot.
articles.stand: Almost nothing about scoliosis is an emergency. The most useful thing you can do in the first week is gather information and slow down.
key: Get the **four facts**: curve size, curve location, skeletal maturity, and date of measurement.
Most curves do not need surgery and many need only monitoring.
Bracing decisions are time-sensitive in a growing child. That part should not drift.
Avoid searching image results. They show the extreme end and are not representative.

blocks.t: The four facts to write down
Before doing anything else, make sure you have these, in writing, from whoever made the diagnosis.

items: **The Cobb angle**, and which curve it refers to if there is more than one.
**The location and direction**, for example a right thoracic curve.
**Skeletal maturity**, usually the Risser grade, or an estimate of remaining growth.
**The date** the X-ray was taken, since everything later is compared against it.

blocks.t: With those four, any clinician can orient themselves quickly. Without them, every new appointment starts from nothing.
Some perspective, quickly

Around 2 to 3 in 100 adolescents have a curve. The large majority never require surgery, and many never require active treatment at all beyond periodic review. The images that come up in a search are the severe end of a wide spectrum.
Your child is very unlikely to be at that end, and being shown those pictures in the first week is a specific, avoidable harm.
What is genuinely time-sensitive

One thing does deserve urgency. If the curve is in the range where bracing may be indicated and the child is still growing, that decision sits in a window that closes as growth finishes. Delaying it by months to think it over can remove the option.
Everything else, choosing a clinic, starting exercise, reading, second opinions, can be done at a sensible pace.
Questions worth asking

items: Given the size and the remaining growth, what is the realistic risk of progression?
When should this be re-measured, and by whom?
Is bracing indicated now, or is there a threshold at which it would be?
What would change the plan?

blocks.t: Talking to your child about it
Plainly, and without catastrophe. Most adolescents cope well when they know what the curve is, what the plan is, and what would change it. They cope badly with overheard anxiety and vague dread.
It also helps to say early that this is something they will end up managing themselves, because that is true and it sets the expectation from the start.

articles.title: What happens in a 60-minute assessment
articles.blurb: A full hour, most of it spent measuring and watching you move.
articles.desc: A step-by-step account of a scoliosis assessment at Rayhab: history, measurement, movement testing, and the plan you leave with.
articles.stand: Knowing what the hour contains makes it easier to arrive prepared and to judge afterwards whether it was worth it.
key: The appointment is an hour, and most of it is assessment rather than treatment.
Posture, curve pattern, trunk rotation, mobility, strength and breathing are all examined.
You leave with findings explained and a plan, not a diagnosis withheld for next time.
Bring any imaging you already have. You do not need to obtain new imaging first.

blocks.t: The conversation first

It starts with history: when the curve was noticed, by whom, what has been measured before, what treatment has happened, what activities matter to you, and what specifically brought you in. That last answer shapes everything, because the plan for someone worried about progression differs from the plan for someone whose back aches by the evening.
Looking and measuring
Then the physical assessment. This is done in clothing that allows the back to be seen, so bring something you can be assessed and move in.

items: **Standing posture** from behind and the side, noting shoulder and pelvis level and how the trunk sits over the pelvis.
**Forward bend with a scoliometer**, measuring trunk rotation in degrees.
**Curve pattern**, establishing where the apex sits and which way it rotates.
**Photographs against a grid**, with your consent, so later comparison is against a record rather than a memory.
**Any existing X-rays**, reviewed and the Cobb angle confirmed.

blocks.t: Watching you move

Static posture is only part of it. Spinal and hip mobility, the ability to actively correct and hold, trunk strength and endurance, breathing pattern and chest expansion, and how the trunk behaves under load and when fatigued all get examined.
For athletes this extends into sport-specific positions, because the plan has to work where the loading actually happens.
The explanation

Findings are explained during the appointment, with the images and numbers in front of you. This part matters. A number you do not understand is not information, and people manage conditions they understand considerably better.
What you leave with

items: A clear statement of what was found and what it means.
An initial home programme, taught rather than handed over on paper.
A review point, and what will be re-measured at it.
Where relevant, a recommendation about onward referral, such as for imaging or a bracing opinion.

blocks.t: If a curve is outside what rehabilitation should be managing alone, you will be told that at the first appointment rather than after a course of treatment.

articles.title: Do you need an X-ray before your first visit?
articles.blurb: No. Bring one if you have it, but do not delay the appointment to obtain one.
articles.desc: Whether imaging is required before a scoliosis assessment, what an X-ray adds, and how radiation exposure is weighed.
articles.stand: This question delays a lot of first appointments unnecessarily, so here is the direct answer.
key: You do not need an X-ray to be assessed. Bring one if you already have it.
An X-ray gives the Cobb angle and skeletal maturity, which nothing else provides.
Trunk rotation, posture, strength and mobility are all assessable without imaging.
Imaging is requested when it would change the plan, not routinely.

blocks.t: The direct answer

No. The assessment goes ahead without imaging, and you will be told honestly afterwards whether an X-ray would change anything. Waiting several weeks to arrange one before being seen usually costs more than it gains.
What an X-ray does provide

items: **The Cobb angle**, which cannot be obtained any other way and which treatment thresholds are built on.
**Skeletal maturity**, via the Risser sign, which is central to judging progression risk.
**Curve structure**, including whether a curve is structural or compensatory.
**A baseline** for later comparison, if one does not already exist.

blocks.t: That is a substantial list, which is why imaging is often appropriate at some point in a growing adolescent. It is not a reason to obtain one before a first conversation.
What can be assessed without it

A great deal: trunk rotation with a scoliometer, curve pattern and direction, posture and trunk balance, mobility, strength, endurance, breathing, and how you move under load. That is enough to start a programme and enough to judge whether onward referral is needed.
The radiation question

A spinal X-ray is a small dose, but adolescents with scoliosis may be imaged repeatedly over years, so the total matters and is worth minimising sensibly. Modern imaging protocols and low-dose systems have reduced exposure considerably.
The reasonable position is neither to avoid imaging nor to repeat it reflexively: image when the result would change a decision, and use the longest interval consistent with safe monitoring.
If you already have imaging

Bring it, including older films if you have them. A sequence of measurements over time is considerably more informative than any single image, because it shows direction of travel rather than a snapshot.
Please do not email imaging or reports before being told how to share them securely.

articles.title: What we measure, and what we re-measure
articles.blurb: If progress is not recorded, it is being remembered. Memory is not a measurement.
articles.desc: The measurements taken at a Rayhab scoliosis assessment and repeated at review, and why change is judged against a record rather than recollection.
articles.stand: Rehabilitation without measurement becomes a matter of opinion, and opinion is a poor guide over years.
key: Measurements are taken at baseline and repeated at defined review points.
Trunk rotation, posture, mobility, strength and function are all tracked.
The Cobb angle comes from imaging and is not re-measured at every review.
Some things will not have changed, and the record says so.

blocks.t: Why measure at all

Change in scoliosis is slow. Over months, perception drifts: a good day feels like progress, a sore week feels like deterioration, and nobody can reliably recall what their shoulder looked like in March.
A record removes that. It also protects you from a clinic telling you things are improving when they are not, which is the more important reason.
What gets measured

items: **Trunk rotation** in degrees, using a scoliometer at defined levels.
**Standing posture**, photographed against a grid with consent, in a repeatable position.
**Trunk balance**, how the head and trunk sit over the pelvis.
**Mobility**, spinal and hip range relevant to the corrections being trained.
**Strength and endurance**, particularly the ability to hold a correction over time and under load.
**Breathing**, chest expansion and the ability to direct breath into the collapsed regions.
**Function**, the tasks you specifically came in unable to tolerate.

blocks.t: Where the Cobb angle fits

The Cobb angle comes from imaging and therefore is not repeated at every review. It is tracked when imaging is done for clinical reasons, and interpreted with measurement error in mind: a change of a few degrees between films may be noise rather than progression.
When it is repeated

Review intervals depend on situation. A growing adolescent in a period of rapid change is reviewed more often than an adult managing symptoms. The interval is set at the outset so the review is planned rather than prompted by worry.
Reporting it honestly
Some reviews show improvement. Some show no change. Some, particularly through a growth spurt, show a curve that has progressed despite everything being done properly.
All three get reported as they are. A record that only ever contains good news is not a record, and the point of measuring is to make it possible to change course when something is not working.
